parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what magnetic flux density $B$ actually measures - the strength of the magnetic effect in terms of the mechanical force it can exert on a wire carrying current.
Hint 2: Recall that the force is largest when the wire is at right angles to the field, and build the unit up from $1\text{ N}$ of force, $1\text{ A}$ of current and $1\text{ m}$ of length.
parts.proper_answer: 1 T is the magnetic flux density that exerts a force of $1\text{ N}$ on a $1\text{ m}$ length of wire carrying a current of $1\text{ A}$ perpendicular / normal to the field.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link B to force, current and length**
Imagine placing a wire carrying current $I$ in a magnetic field. The field pushes on the moving charges, so the wire feels a force $F$ proportional to $B$, to $I$ and to the length $L$ in the field. That is why the tesla can be defined mechanically rather than just as lines per area.

Step 2: **Add the perpendicular condition**
The force is maximum when the wire is at $90^{\circ}$ to the field lines, because only the component of field perpendicular to the current contributes. So: $$1\text{ T} = 1\text{ N A}^{-1}\text{ m}^{-1}$$ for a wire perpendicular to the field. In words, one tesla gives one newton per ampere per metre when $I$ is normal to $B$.

parts.label: (b)
(b)(i)
parts.text: Determine the magnetic flux density $B$, in $\text{mT}$.
hints: Hint 1: Focus only on side PQ first - it is the only length in the field. Note its length in metres, the current through it from P to Q, and the size of the extra magnetic force from the newton meter change.
Hint 2: Relate the magnetic force to $B$, $I$, the length in the field and $\sin$ of the angle between current and field seen in Fig. 8.2, then rearrange to find $B$ and convert to mT.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Pick out the active wire**
Only PQ is in the uniform field at first. Current flows along PQ from P to Q. Length is $$L = 6.0\text{ cm} = 0.060\text{ m}$$ Current $$I = 5.0\text{ A}$$ Magnetic force magnitude equals the change in balance reading: $$F = 1.0\text{ mN} = 1.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$$

Step 2: **Use the angled-wire rule**
From the top view the current and the horizontal $B$ field are at $50^{\circ}$ to each other, not $90^{\circ}$. The general force law is: $$F = BIL\sin\theta$$ where $\theta$ is the angle between $I$ and $B$. Here $\theta = 50^{\circ}$.

Step 3: **Rearrange and calculate**
Rearrange before substituting: $$B = \frac{F}{IL\sin\theta}$$ Then: $$B = \frac{1.0\times 10^{-3}}{5.0 \times 0.060 \times \sin 50^{\circ}} \approx 4.4\times 10^{-3}\text{ T}$$ So $$B \approx 4.4\text{ mT}$$ to 2 s.f.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State, with a reason, whether the change in the reading on the newton meter is an increase or a decrease.
hints: Hint 1: Picture the top view with current P to Q to the right and $B$ at $50^{\circ}$ to it - apply Fleming's left-hand rule with First finger along $B$ and Second finger along current to find whether the resulting force on PQ points up or down.
parts.proper_answer: Decrease, because the magnetic force on PQ acts vertically upwards, reducing the tension that the newton meter must support.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the force direction**
Both $I$ along PQ and $B$ are horizontal, so $I \times B$ must be vertical. Using Fleming's left-hand rule, with the field component across the current, the force on the P to Q current comes out vertically upwards. An upward magnetic push helps support the weight of the frame, so the pull on the newton meter falls. That is a decrease in reading.

parts.text:
The frame is lowered further so that the vertical sides start to enter the magnetic field.

Suggest what effect this will have on the frame.

markscheme_points.text: frame will rotate (so that PQ beco

hints: Hint 1: Compare the current directions in the two vertical sides - one carries current down, the other carries it up - and think about what pair of opposite Fleming's left-hand forces in a horizontal field will do to a freely suspended frame.
parts.proper_answer: The frame will rotate / twist about a vertical axis due to opposite lateral forces on the two vertical sides forming a couple.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the couple**
Once the vertical sides enter the horizontal field, they carry opposite currents. Fleming's left-hand rule gives opposite horizontal forces on the left and right sides. Two equal, opposite, separated forces make a couple, so the freely suspended frame cannot stay still - it twists and rotates until the forces balance in a new orientation.
